sections.section_title: The Tradition of Religious Tolerance and Royal Patronage
sections.content:
Chapter I
SECTARIAN
DEVELOPMENTS
(Śaiva and Vaisnava)
(1)
India is well known for its spirit of religious tolerance,
and this has been the case since the dawn of recorded
history. The kings who have ruled this land as well as the
people who have lived here have always exemplified the
principle of peaceful co-existence of religious ideologies
and practices. Every state in the country presents a happy
mosaic of all the religions and cults that are prevalent in
the country and elsewhere. Strife on account of bigotry,
fanaticism and discrimination in the name of religion has
been rare and unusual. Accommodation with a respect for
the viewpoints of others has always been held out as a
virtue, especially in social and religious matters.
The history of the land has partly been responsible for
this desirable detail in the inclinations of the people. The
royal dynasties that have held sway over the fortunes of
the several regions, have in most cases taken care not to
espouse the cause of any one religion at the expense of
others; and they have never been guilty of suppressing a
religious doctrine or custom, however inimical to their
own. While expressing devotion to their own faith either
by making endowments on a shrine already existing or by
sponsoring a new shrine, they simultaneously encouraged
other faiths. And it often happened in royal house-holds
that the king's personal preference was for one faith while
the queen's was for another, without however disturbing
domestic peace and harmony. It was quite common for the
son to follow one religion in his private life while his
father did another, and this would not be taken amiss
either by the parties themselves or by the people.
It is difficult, therefore, to ascertain the personal
religious inclinations or convictions of a ruler or chieftain
by the shrines that he sponsored or supported. This has
been so from the earliest of times. Consider the case of
the great monarch Aśoka himself. Discounting the stories
of his conversion to Buddhism (for which there is hardly
any historical evidence), he not only supported the cause
of Buddhist religion, but made endowments to the Jaina
and Ajivika sects. His inscriptions refer to his concern for
the sramana as well as the brāhmaņa groups. Likewise,
Kanişka and Harśa-vardhana patronized all religious sects,
including the folk cults.
In Karnataka, to take an illustrative example of the
states, the Sātāvahana kings (first three centuries A.D.)
were Śaivas, but they built many Buddhist shrines (like
the Tara-Bhagavati temple in Balligāme) and monuments
(like the stūpas near Kolhapur). Likewise, the Kadambas,
who were by preference devotees of Śiva, adored also
Vişnu and Jina, and their capital Banavāsi was a great
centre of Buddhism. The Kadamba rulers were avid
followers of the Vedic religion, but Kākutstha-Varma
(425-445 A.D.) Bestowed land grants on the Jaina ascetic
Śruta-kirti. Mrgeśa-varma (470-488 A.D.) gave grants for
Jaina shrines and Ravi-varma (500-538 A.D.) built a
Jinālaya at Palasikā (Halasī) in Belgaum district. The
Gangas of Talakādu were Jainas, but many temples to Siva
and Vişnu were built by them. The Badami Calūkyan
ruler Mangaļīśa is renowned for the excellent rock-
cut shrine for Visnu ('Vişnu-grha') which he got
excavated in 578 A.D., but he was a zealous devotee of
Śiva (Mahākuțeśvara). His predecessor, Krrti-varma I,
(elder brother) had been a devotee of Visnu, and had
conceived this shrine.
The Alupa rulers of Tuļunādu (about 660 A.D.) were
mainly Śaivas and a few of them were Jainas; but they
built shrines for Vişņu and Śakti also, and encouraged
the Natha-siddha cult. Hoysaļa monarch, Bittiga-
Vişnuvardhana (1108-1152), who built the famous Keśava
temple at Belür, was in personal life a Jaina (the story of
his conversion to Śrīvaişņava faith by Rāmānuja is without
foundation), and built many basad is also. The Kalyāna
Cāļukyan ruler, Vikramāditya VI (1076-1127), was a
zealour devotee of Śiva, but endowed munificently to the
Buddhist vıhāra at Dambaļa and the temple to Tārā-
Bhagavati. The splendid temple to Śiva at Jalasangavi (in
ruins now), built by him, contains most impressive
sculptural representations of Visņu. The celebrated
Vijayanagar monarch Krişņadeva-rāya (1509-1530) was
a Vaisnava in his personal predilections, but has made rich
endowments to the Śiva temples at Kāļahasti, Kāñcīpuram
and other places.
This is true of almost every other state in the country.
Royal patronage ignored sectarian differences, and
respected religious devotion in whatever form and to
whichever divinity.
sections.summary: This section argues that India has a historical tradition of religious tolerance and peaceful co-existence. It posits that Indian kings and dynasties, regardless of their personal faith, consistently patronized a multitude of religions, including Buddhism, Jainism, Śaivism, and Vaiṣṇavism. Numerous historical examples, primarily from Karnataka (Sātavāhanas, Kadambas, Cālukyas, Hoysaḷas) and other regions (Aśoka, Kaniṣka), are provided to demonstrate that rulers often supported faiths different from their own, making it difficult to determine a monarch's personal beliefs solely from their endowments. This widespread, non-exclusive patronage is presented as a foundational characteristic of Indian history.

sections.section_title: Inscriptional Evidence for Syncretism and a Unified Godhead
sections.content:
In more recent times, the rulers of the states and
principalities promoted the cause of alien creeds also,
like-Islam, Christianity, Zoroastrianism and Judaism,
which had entered into the country's commonwealth of
religions.
This policy of not only religious tolerance but active
encouragement of all religions was followed by all the
ruling dynasties and their feudatories in the several regions
of the country. This was in view of the fact that the
population, although always divided among diverse
religious denominations, managed to live amicably.
Religious beliefs and practices were relevant within
households and sectarian communities, but the social,
political and economic life of the people transcended these
confines. People had the wisdom to recognise that all
religions were different approaches to the same Godhead
(who is one and undivided), and to treat religions other
than theirs with as much respect as they bestowed on their
own. The rulers and other administrators realized that
their subjects who would be happy if all religions were
uniformly encouraged and supported. But then, it was not
merely as a calculated expedient that this was done. The
spirit of religious tolerance permeated the entire social
fabric, among all classes of people and at all levels. There
are numerous inscriptions and other literary records that
eloquently pronounce the oneness of the Godhead and the
equal merit of all religions that approach this one God.
A splendid example of this outlook is this verse in an
inscription assigned to 642 A.D.:
यो विश्वं वेदवेद्यं जननजलनिधेर्भागिनः पारदृश्वा ।
पौर्यापर्याविरुद्धं वचनमनुपमं निष्कलंकं यदियम्।
तं वन्दे साधुवन्द्यं सकलगुणनिधिं ध्वस्तदोषं द्विषन्तम्।
बुद्धं वा वर्धमानं शतदलनिलयं वा केशवं वा शिवं वा ॥
The verse makes obesience to that principle, free from
all defects, full of all merit and whose doctrine is
imcomparably pure and elevating, whether it be Buddha,
Vardhamāna (Jina), Brahmā, Vişnu, or Śiva.
Another example is from an inscription of the Hoysaļa
period in Belūr in Karnataka:
यं शैवाः समुपासते शिव इति ब्रह्मोति वेदान्तिनः ।
बौद्धा बुद्ध इति प्रमाणपटवः कर्तेति नैयायिकाः।
अर्हन्नित्यथ जैनशासनरता कर्मेति मीमांसकाः ।
सोऽयं वो विदधातु वांछितफलं त्रैलौक्यनाथो विभुः ॥
"May he, the lord of the three worlds the all powerful
God, bestow on all of you the fulfillment of all desires,
that one God whom the Śaivites worship as Śiva, the
Vedāntins regard as Brahman, the Buddhists adore as the
Buddha, the Naiyāyikas conceptualise as the Maker, the
Jainas worship as Jina (Arhat) and the Mīmāmsakas speak
of as karma".
Still another example is from an inscription dated 1151
A.D. from Kaidāļa (Tumkur district), also in Karnataka:
जयन्ति यस्यावदातोऽपि भारती।
विभूतयस्तिर्थकृतोऽपि नैह्निते
शिवाय धात्रे सुगताय विष्णवे ।
जिनाय तस्मै सकलात्मने नमः ॥
Here also, obeisance is paid to the one principle, which
is all comprehending, and which manifests itself as Śiva,
Brahmā, Sugata (Buddha), Vişnu and Jina.
sections.summary: This section reinforces the theme of religious tolerance by citing direct inscriptional evidence. It argues that this spirit of accommodation extended even to 'alien creeds' like Islam and Christianity in later periods. The core of this section presents several Sanskrit verses from historical inscriptions (dated 642 A.D., Hoysala period, and 1151 A.D.) that explicitly state the oneness of the ultimate Godhead, which is worshipped under different names (Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Buddha, Jina) by various sects. These inscriptions serve as primary evidence for a pervasive syncretic philosophy where different religions were seen as valid paths to the same divine principle.

sections.section_title: The Rise and Decline of the Traipuruṣa (Trinity) Cult
sections.content:
Kokkalla-māharāja while causing the praśasti of Nagara
to be inscribed began with a prayer to the all-comprehensive
eternal God who is described variously as Śiva, Brahmā,
Buddha, Jina and Vamana (Vişnu) (cf. Epigraphica Indica,
149-150):
यं वेदान्तविदो वदन्ति मनसः संकल्पभूतं शिवम् ।
ब्रह्मकं परमक्षरं तमजरं तंश्वामरं तद्विदुः ।
अन्ये तं शिवमेव बुद्धममलं त्वन्ये जिनं वामनम्।
तस्मै सर्वमयैक्यकारणपते सर्वाय नित्याय नमः ॥
Broadly, however, the country has witnessed the growth
of four religious sects (called samayas) with their own
practices and customs and doctrines: Jainism, Buddhism,
Śaivism (with its divisions Śaiva, Pāśupata and Kāpālika)
and Vaisnavism.
बौद्धं चाप्यार्हतं चैव शैवं पाशुपतं तथा ।
कापालं पांचरात्रंच षडेते समयाः स्मृताः ॥
(Vīrāgama, 1, 77)
बौद्धं चैवार्हतं चैव पांचरात्रं च शैवकम्।
समयं चतुर्विधं स्यात्तु तत्तद्भदमनेकधा ।
(Acintyāgama, 40, 5-6)
And many kings of the dynasties that have ruled in
various regions of the country have proudly claimed in
their inscriptions to be "supporters of four observances
and doctrines" ("catus-samaya-samuddharana"), Temples
to Śiva, Vişnu, Jina and Buddha were often constructed
together in several states, as for instance, in Kadiyūr in
Karnataka (“catus-samaya-devatā-nilaya" as an inscription
dated 929 A.D. informs us (Epigraphica India, Vol. 13, p.
329). Sometimes, Brahmā, the creator, is also provided a
shrine for himself, as in Puskara in the northern region
and Balligāme in the South (inscription dated 1129, "Hari-
Hara-Kamalāsana-Vitarāga-Baud-dhalayangal"). It is
interesting that the Balligame inscription speaks of these
five doctrines as the "five streams irrigating the earth"
("vasundharegeseva pañca-śaradantire") or socio-religious
organisations or communities. An earlier inscription (dated
1022) found at Belür, Karnataka, of Jayasimha, refers to
a temple for three divinities (traipuruśa, viz. Brahmā,
Vişnu and Śiva) built by Akkadevī, but the inscription
mentions that she practised the rituals of Jina, Buddha,
Ananta (viz. Visņu) and Rudra (viz. Siva). The Şikāripura
inscription of 1048 A.D. mentions that an officer, Nāga-
varma, built four shrines, one each to Jina, Vişņu, Śiva
and Muni (Viz. Śākyamuni or Buddha).
Of these persuations, Jainism and Buddhism were
movements that originated in northern India and arrived
in the South during the centuries prior to the Christian era,
as a result of some adventitious historical circumstances
and occurrences. Indeed, they did not originate as distinct
creeds, but only as divisions of the mainstream; it is
several centuries later that they assumed distinct postures.
The cults of Śiva and Vişnu were not movements like
Jainism and Buddhism, but were more or less indigenous
to the population here. Whatever their origin, they spread
among the people imperceptibly and widely along with
the folk ideology in times more ancient than recorded
history. The worship of Śiva and Vişņu, sometimes along
with Brahmā, by people at large is as old as the folklore
and myths that provided material for the purānas.
Brahmā as self-born (svayam-bhu) and creator of the
world, Visnu as the preserver of the world, and Śiva as
the destroyer (at the time of universal dissolution or
pralaya) constitute the 'trinity' (traipuruśa) or three aspects
of the Godhead, that appear to have been adored in the
country during the early historic period. Later, the worship
of Brahma became obsolete, and the other two divinities
came to have their own wide-spread cults, which have
continued till our own day. But Brahmā appears to have
continued to receive worship till about the 9th century. We
have an inscription dated 866 A.D. which begins with a
verse adoring all three deities (Epigraphica India, Vol.6,
p. 102):
During the period of the early Cāļukyas (of Bādāmi),
it was usual for the temple to have three cells (tri-kūțacala)
to accommodate the three divinities, Brahmā, Vişnu and
Śiva, collectively called 'tri-puruśa' ('traipuruśa' or 'trayi-
puruśa').
Several inscriptions contain reverential references to
all three gods together. For instance, the 'praśasti' of the
Nepali monarch Siddhi-nrsimha-malla (son of Harihara-
simha) in the medieval times, begins with this verse:
ब्रह्मत्वे सृजते विश्वं स्थितौ पालयते हरिः ।
रुद्ररूपाय कल्पान्ते नमस्तुभ्यं त्रिमूर्तयो ।
Obesience is paid here to the three forms of the same
god, who as Brahma creates the world, as Vişņu preserves
the world and as Śiva destroys at the end of the aeon (cf.
Inscriptions of Nepal, p. 23-26).
The stone-inscription in Śiva's temple in Madha-pura
has this verse in a similar vein:
सर्गस्थितिलयहेतोर्विश्वस्य ब्रह्मविष्णुरुद्राणाम्।
मूर्तित्रयं प्रदधते संसारभिदे नमो विभवे ॥
The famous rock-cut shrine dedicated to Visņu ('Visņu-
gṛha') at Bādāmi (Cave 3), constructed or completed by
the Cāļukyan ruler Mangaļīśa in 578 A.D. is actually a
shrine for all three divinities; Vişnu is the central deity
and he is flanked by Brahmā on the right and Śiva on the
left. The Vijayeśvara temple (now known as Jambulinga
temple), built by the king of the same dynasty, Vijayāditya
(696-733), in memory of his mother Vinayavati, in Bādāmi
was again a 'trai-puruśa' shrine; the pillar inscription in
the temple mentions that all the three deities were installed
there. The Konti-gudi and the Huccap-payya-matha (gudi)
in Aihole are Śiva shrines, but Śiva as the central deity
is flanked by Vişnu on the right and Brahma on the left.
The Trikūțeśvara temple at Gadag, built during the days
of the Calukyas of Kalyāņa, has three lingas representing
Brahmā, Śiva and Vişņu. The Tryambakeśvara temple
complex at Aihole and the
Banasankari temple at Annigeri are likewise for all
three deities.
The practice of building 'trai-puruśa' temples seems
to have died out after the eighth century, Brahmā having
ceased to receive independent adoration from the
people. There seems to have been many shrines con-
jointly dedicated to Śiva and Vişņu. An inscription of the
eleventh century found in Devpād village (Rājśāhi in
Bengal) speaks of a temple of this sort dedicated to
Pradyumneśvara:
लक्ष्मीवल्लभ-शैलजादयितयोरद्वैतलीलगृहम्।
प्रद्युम्नेश्वर-शब्दलांछनमधिष्ठानं नमुस्कुर्महे ।
यत्रालिगंमभंग-कातरतया स्थित्वान्तरे कान्तयो-
र्देवीभ्यां कथमप्यभिन्नतनुता शिल्पेऽन्तरायः कृतः ॥
sections.summary: This section narrows the focus to the specific theological developments within mainstream Hinduism. It discusses the major religious sects ('samayas') like Jainism, Buddhism, Śaivism, and Vaiṣṇavism. The central theme is the rise of the 'traipuruṣa' concept, the worship of the trinity of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, often housed together in three-celled temples ('tri-kūṭācala'). The text provides examples of such temples from Bādāmi, Aihole, and Gadag. It then charts the decline of this practice after the 8th century as the worship of Brahmā became obsolete, leading to the rise of shrines jointly dedicated to Śiva and Viṣṇu, a precursor to more distinct sectarian developments.

sections.section_title: The Crystallisation of Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava Cults through Āgamas
sections.content:
This temple which has been described as 'advaita-
līlāgrha' was built by Vijaya-sena.
Śiva and Vişnu shrines began to be separately
constructed, although the composite icon of Hari-Hara (or
Śankara-Nārāyana) came into vogue. A separate shrine to
this composite deity was built in 1223 by Polāļva, (a
minister of the Hoysaļa king, Narasimha II), in Harihara
(Citradurga district, Karnataka). There is another shrine
in Kodagi-Shankaranārāyaņa (in Tuļunādu) built in the
thirteenth century (where worship is offered to a pair of
lingas instead of to a composite deity). There are several
other shrines in Tuļunādu in Karnataka to the composite
deity, like those at Pāņdeśvara, Bārkūru, Kodavūru and
Nandavara. They are structures which are later than the
fifteenth century. But it is more usual for Śiva and Vişnu
shrines to occur independently. The reason is the branching
out of the Saiva and Vaisnava creeds as exclusive and
distinct cults, with their own Agamas prescribing
characteristic customs and practices, philosophies and
orientations.
The crystallisation of the cults was facilitated by the
emergence and prevalence of 'agamas' around the seventh
and eighth centuries. The 'agamas' are definitive and
prescriptive texts in Sanskrit, dealing mainly with worship
in temples, but dealing also with worship at home and
general conduct. When temples came into being, and
became popular among the people, the need was felt for
priests to discharge the role of worshippers on behalf of
the people or as mediators between the divine being and
man. There was now also a class of professional temple-
priests who sought to fill this role, and it is for their benefit
and guidance that the agamas came to be prepared. It is
probable that the bulk of the agamas were composed
during the Pallava and early Cola periods in the Tamil
country.
The division of the agamas was mainly according to
the divinity installed and worshipped in the temple. Thus
we have different sets of agamas relating to Śiva
(Śaivāgamas) and to Vişnu (Vaisnavāgamas). There
were also āgama texts, belonging to earlier periods,
dealing with the worship of Jina and Buddha. The latter
became important when the Māhāyāna sects arose and
flourished. The Jaina-āgamas were meant not only to
prescribe worship rituals for the tirthanikaras (Jinas), but
for their attendant yaksas and yakşiņīs. The Bauddha-
āgamas (forming part of Vajrayāna-tantras) concerned
themselves with the methods and details of worship of the
Bodhisattvas (like Avalokiteśvara) and folk deities (like
Hārīti).
It is curious that the early references to temples and
temple-worship do not include the worship of Śakti or
mother goddess. But there can hardly be any doubt that
this was prevalent among the people from time immemorial.
There must have been folk-shrines to the village-goddesses,
but they could not have compared favourably with the
rock-cut or structural temples that came to be constructed
because of royal patronage. Among deities worshipped in
formal temples, goddesses came to be included only at a
later stage. The Sātavāhana inscriptions (for instance, the
Nānāghat inscription of Nāganikā, queen of Satakarņi II,
184-125 B.C.) mention only male deities (Indra,
Sankarśaņa, Vāsudeva, the guardians of quarters, the god
of death, the god of wealth, etc.). But Hala's Gāthā-
saptaśatī, belonging to a slightly later date but composed
during the reign of the Satavāhanas, begins with an
invocation to Śiva (Paśupati), husband of Gauri.
पसुवइणो रोसारुणपडिमासंकांत गोरिमुहअन्दं।
गहिअग्धपंकअं विअ संझासलिलांजलिं णमह ॥
ईपशुपते रोषारुणप्रतिमासंक्रान्तगौरीमुखचन्द्रम्।
गृहीतार्धपंकजमिव सन्ध्यासलिलांजलिं नमता ।।उ
(1.1)
The earliest monumental shrine to a goddess in South
India was also erected during the Satavāhana period: the
shrine to Tārā-bhagavati at Balligāme. The recognition of
mother-goddesses as worthy of formal and structural
temples, and customary and elaborate worship was probably
due to the influence of the Māhāyāna variety of Buddhism,
which conceptualized the power of Buddha, the
enlightenment and the mission of the Bodhisattvas in
terms of female divinities. The Jaina ideology of yakṣiṇīs
also must have helped.
sections.summary: This final section explains the mechanism behind the divergence of Śaivism and Vaiṣṇavism into distinct sects: the emergence of the Āgamas. These prescriptive Sanskrit texts, which appeared around the 7th-8th centuries, codified temple worship, rituals, and philosophy for specific deities. This led to the construction of separate shrines for Śiva and Viṣṇu, although the syncretic Hari-Hara form also gained prominence. The section notes that Āgamas existed for Jainism and Buddhism as well. It concludes by briefly discussing the worship of the mother goddess (Śakti), suggesting it was an ancient folk tradition that was integrated into formal temple worship at a later stage, possibly influenced by Mahāyāna Buddhist and Jaina concepts of female divinities.

chapter_summary: Chapter I, 'Sectarian Developments (Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava)', argues that India's history is fundamentally characterized by religious tolerance and syncretism. The author asserts that from ancient times, rulers and dynasties across the subcontinent patronized a wide array of faiths—including Jainism, Buddhism, Śaivism, and Vaiṣṇavism—often irrespective of their personal beliefs. This argument is substantiated with numerous examples of royal endowments and inscriptional verses that praise a single, universal Godhead worshipped under various names. The chapter then traces the evolution from the collective worship of the Hindu trinity (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva) in 'traipuruṣa' temples to the eventual decline of Brahmā's cult. This shift paved the way for the rise of distinct Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava sects, a process that was formalized and crystallized by the emergence of the Āgamas around the 7th-8th centuries. These texts codified the unique rituals and philosophies of each sect, leading to the construction of separate temples and the establishment of distinct religious identities.
key_arguments: India has a long and continuous history of religious tolerance, where conflict based on religion has been 'rare and unusual'.
Royal patronage was typically non-exclusive, with rulers supporting multiple religious sects simultaneously, making it difficult to ascertain their personal faith from endowments alone.

Numerous inscriptions from different periods and regions explicitly articulate a syncretic worldview, viewing various deities (Śiva, Viṣṇu, Buddha, Jina) as manifestations of a single, ultimate reality.

The worship of the Hindu trinity (traipuruṣa) in dedicated three-shrine temples was a significant practice in the early medieval period, which declined after the 8th century due to the obsolescence of Brahmā's cult.

The development of distinct Āgamic texts (Śaivāgamas, Vaiṣṇavāgamas) around the 7th-8th centuries was the primary catalyst for the crystallization of Śaivism and Vaiṣṇavism into separate, exclusive cults with standardized rituals and philosophies.
key_takeaways: The narrative of widespread religious conflict in pre-modern India is challenged in favor of a model of pervasive tolerance and mutual respect.
The religious identity of ancient and medieval Indian rulers was often fluid and inclusive, reflected in their patronage patterns.
Syncretism was not just a folk phenomenon but was articulated in official royal inscriptions.
Sectarian identities in Hinduism were not static but evolved over time, with a key turning point being the decline of trinity worship and the rise of Āgama-based practices.
The Āgamas played a crucial role in transforming broad religious leanings into structured, codified sects with professional priesthoods.

historical_figures.name: Aśoka
historical_figures.significance: Patronized Buddhist, Jaina, and Ājīvika sects, showing broad religious support.
historical_figures.dates: c. 268 to 232 BCE (not specified in text)

historical_figures.name: Kaniṣka
historical_figures.significance: Patronized all religious sects, including folk cults.
historical_figures.dates: c. 127 to 150 AD (not specified in text)

historical_figures.name: Harṣa-vardhana
historical_figures.significance: Patronized all religious sects, including folk cults.
historical_figures.dates: c. 606 to 647 AD (not specified in text)

historical_figures.name: Sātāvahana kings
historical_figures.significance: Identified as Śaivas, but built many Buddhist shrines.

historical_figures.name: Kākutstha-Varma
historical_figures.significance: Follower of Vedic religion who gave land grants to a Jaina ascetic.

historical_figures.name: Śruta-kīrti
historical_figures.significance: Recipient of a land grant from Kākutstha-Varma.

historical_figures.name: Mṛgeśa-varma
historical_figures.significance: Gave grants for Jaina shrines.

historical_figures.name: Ravi-varma
historical_figures.significance: Built a Jinālaya (Jain temple).

historical_figures.name: Maṅgalīśa
historical_figures.significance: A devotee of Śiva who excavated a famous rock-cut shrine for Viṣṇu.

historical_figures.name: Kṛtti-varma I
historical_figures.significance: Predecessor and elder brother of Maṅgalīśa; a devotee of Viṣṇu who conceived the Viṣṇu shrine.

historical_figures.name: Biṭṭiga-Viṣṇuvardhana
historical_figures.significance: Built the Keśava temple at Belūr but was personally a Jaina.

historical_figures.name: Rāmānuja
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in the context of the (disputed) story of Viṣṇuvardhana's conversion.

historical_figures.name: Vikramāditya VI
historical_figures.significance: A devotee of Śiva who endowed a Buddhist vihāra and built a Śiva temple with sculptures of Viṣṇu.

historical_figures.name: Kṛṣṇadeva-rāya
historical_figures.significance: A Vaiṣṇava who made rich endowments to Śiva temples.

historical_figures.name: Kokkalla-māharāja
historical_figures.significance: His praśasti (eulogy inscription) begins with a prayer to an all-comprehensive God.

historical_figures.name: Jayasimha
historical_figures.significance: His inscription of 1022 refers to a 'traipuruṣa' temple built by Akkadevī.

historical_figures.name: Akkadevī
historical_figures.significance: Built a temple for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, while practicing rituals of Jina, Buddha, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.

historical_figures.name: Nāga-varma
historical_figures.significance: Built four shrines for Jina, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Buddha.

historical_figures.name: Siddhi-nṛsiṁha-malla
historical_figures.significance: His 'praśasti' contains a verse adoring the trinity.

historical_figures.name: Harihara-siṁha
historical_figures.significance: Father of Siddhi-nṛsiṁha-malla.

historical_figures.name: Vijayāditya
historical_figures.significance: Built the Vijayeśvara ('trai-puruśa') temple in Bādāmi in memory of his mother.

historical_figures.name: Vinayavatī
historical_figures.significance: Mother of Vijayāditya, in whose memory the Vijayeśvara temple was built.

historical_figures.name: Vijaya-sena
historical_figures.significance: Built the 'advaita-līlāgṛha' temple for Pradyumneśvara (joint Śiva-Viṣṇu).

historical_figures.name: Polāļva
historical_figures.role: Minister of Hoysala king Narasimha II
historical_figures.significance: Built a separate shrine for the composite deity Hari-Hara.

historical_figures.name: Narasimha II
historical_figures.significance: King under whom the minister Polāļva served.

historical_figures.name: Nāganikā
historical_figures.significance: Her Nānāghāṭ inscription mentions only male deities.

historical_figures.name: Sātakarni II
historical_figures.significance: Husband of queen Nāganikā.

historical_figures.name: Hāla
historical_figures.significance: Author of Gāthā-saptaśatī which invokes Śiva as husband of Gauri.

historical_events.significance: Early inscription mentioning worship of male deities like Indra, Sankarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva.
Period when Śaiva rulers built Buddhist shrines, showing religious plurality.
A Vedic follower patronizing a Jaina ascetic.
Royal patronage for Jaina shrines.
Construction of a Jain temple by a Kadamba ruler.

historical_events.event: Excavation of Viṣṇu-gṛha (Cave 3) at Bādāmi by Maṅgalīśa
historical_events.significance: A major Cālukyan rock-cut temple dedicated to the trinity, initiated by a Vaiṣṇava and completed by a Śaiva.

historical_events.event: Inscription with syncretic verse praising Buddha, Jina, Viṣṇu, Śiva etc.
historical_events.significance: Early inscriptional evidence for the concept of a single Godhead with multiple forms.

historical_events.event: Rule of Ālupa rulers of Tuḷunāḍu
historical_events.significance: Rulers, mainly Śaiva, built shrines for Viṣṇu and Śakti and encouraged other cults.

historical_events.event: Reign of Vijayāditya and construction of Vijayeśvara temple
historical_events.significance: Building of a 'trai-puruśa' temple in Bādāmi.

historical_events.date: around the seventh and eighth centuries
historical_events.significance: Codification of sectarian worship, leading to the crystallization of distinct cults.
Marks the wane of Brahmā worship and a shift towards more distinct Śaiva/Vaiṣṇava identities.

historical_events.event: Inscription adoring all three deities of the trinity
historical_events.significance: Shows continued worship of Brahmā until at least the 9th century.
Evidence of temples housing deities of four different sects together.
Refers to a 'traipuruṣa' temple built by Akkadevī who followed rituals of five different deities.
An officer builds four separate shrines for Jina, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Buddha.
A Śaiva king patronizing Buddhist sites and including Viṣṇu imagery in a Śiva temple.
A Jaina king building the famous Vaiṣṇava Keśava temple at Belūr.
Refers to shrines for Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, Jina, and Buddha, calling them 'five streams irrigating the earth'.
Pays obeisance to one principle manifesting as Śiva, Brahmā, Buddha, Viṣṇu, and Jina.
Construction of a dedicated temple for the syncretic Śiva-Viṣṇu deity.
A Vaiṣṇava emperor making large grants to Śaiva temples.

geographic_locations.context: The subject of the entire chapter, described as a land of religious tolerance.
geographic_locations.significance: The macro-location for all discussed historical and religious developments.

geographic_locations.context: Used as an illustrative example of religious harmony and royal patronage.
geographic_locations.significance: Many of the key dynasties and inscriptions cited (Sātavāhana, Kadamba, Cālukya, Hoysala) are from this region.

geographic_locations.context: Site of the Tārā-Bhagavatī temple (Buddhist) built by Sātavāhanas. Also site of shrines for five faiths mentioned in a 1129 inscription.
geographic_locations.significance: A key site demonstrating long-term religious pluralism and patronage.

geographic_locations.context: Site of stūpas (Buddhist monuments) built by Sātavāhanas.
geographic_locations.significance: Example of Śaiva rulers supporting Buddhism.

geographic_locations.context: Capital of the Kadambas, described as a great centre of Buddhism.
geographic_locations.significance: Shows a capital city fostering multiple religions under its ruling dynasty.

geographic_locations.context: In Belgaum district, where Ravi-varma built a Jinālaya (Jain temple).
geographic_locations.significance: Specific site of Kadamba patronage to Jainism.

geographic_locations.context: Location of Palasikā.
geographic_locations.significance: Geographic context for Kadamba activity.

geographic_locations.context: Capital of the Gaṅgas, who were Jainas but built many temples to Śiva and Viṣṇu.
geographic_locations.significance: Example of Jaina rulers patronizing Hindu deities.

geographic_locations.context: Site of the famous rock-cut Viṣṇu-gṛha (Cave 3) and the Vijayeśvara temple, both housing the trinity.
geographic_locations.significance: A major centre for the Cālukyas and a prime example of 'traipuruṣa' worship.

geographic_locations.context: Region ruled by the Ālupas. Also location of later Hari-Hara shrines.
geographic_locations.significance: Region showing a mix of Śaiva, Jaina, Vaiṣṇava, and Śakti worship.

geographic_locations.context: Site of the Keśava temple built by Viṣṇuvardhana. Also location of a Hoysala period inscription.
geographic_locations.significance: A major Hoysala center and site of significant Vaiṣṇava architecture and syncretic inscriptions.

geographic_locations.context: Capital of a later Cālukyan dynasty.
geographic_locations.significance: Identifies the dynasty of Vikramāditya VI.

geographic_locations.context: Site of a Buddhist vihāra endowed by Vikramāditya VI.
geographic_locations.significance: Example of a Śaiva king's patronage to Buddhism.

geographic_locations.context: Site of a Śiva temple built by Vikramāditya VI containing impressive Viṣṇu sculptures.
geographic_locations.significance: Demonstrates syncretism within a single temple structure.

geographic_locations.context: Śiva temple that received endowments from the Vaiṣṇava king Kṛṣṇadeva-rāya.
geographic_locations.significance: Example of Vijayanagara cross-sectarian patronage.

geographic_locations.context: Śiva temple that received endowments from the Vaiṣṇava king Kṛṣṇadeva-rāya.
geographic_locations.significance: Example of Vijayanagara cross-sectarian patronage.

geographic_locations.context: In Tumkur district, site of an inscription from 1151 A.D. with a syncretic verse.
geographic_locations.significance: Source of primary inscriptional evidence for religious harmony.

geographic_locations.context: Location of Kaiḍāļa.
geographic_locations.significance: Geographic context for the 1151 A.D. inscription.

geographic_locations.context: Location of the praśasti of Kokkalla-māharāja.
geographic_locations.significance: Source of an inscription praising an all-comprehensive God.

geographic_locations.context: In Karnataka, site of a 'catus-samaya-devatā-nilaya' (shrine for deities of four sects) mentioned in a 929 A.D. inscription.
geographic_locations.significance: Direct evidence of multi-faith temple complexes.

geographic_locations.context: A northern region site with a shrine for Brahmā.
geographic_locations.significance: One of the few remaining centers of Brahmā worship.

geographic_locations.context: Site of a 1048 A.D. inscription mentioning the construction of four shrines.
geographic_locations.significance: Evidence of parallel patronage to four different faiths.

geographic_locations.context: Site of the Konti-guḍi, Huccap-payya-maṭha, and Tryambakeśvara temple complex, showing trinity worship.
geographic_locations.significance: An important Cālukyan center with numerous temples showing sectarian evolution.

geographic_locations.context: Site of the Trikūṭeśvara temple with three lingas for Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu.
geographic_locations.significance: A prime example of a 'tri-kūṭācala' temple dedicated to the trinity.

geographic_locations.context: Site of the Banasaṅkari temple, dedicated to all three deities of the trinity.
geographic_locations.significance: Another example of a trinity temple.

geographic_locations.context: Location of an 11th-century inscription speaking of a joint Śiva-Viṣṇu temple.
geographic_locations.significance: Shows that the trend of joint worship was not confined to South India.

geographic_locations.context: Site of a shrine to the composite deity Hari-Hara, built in 1223.
geographic_locations.significance: An important center for the syncretic Hari-Hara cult.

geographic_locations.context: In Tuḷunāḍu, site of a 13th-century Hari-Hara shrine.
geographic_locations.significance: Another center for the Hari-Hara cult.

geographic_locations.context: Other sites in Tuḷunāḍu with shrines to the composite Hari-Hara deity.
geographic_locations.significance: Shows the popularity of the Hari-Hara cult in this specific region.

geographic_locations.context: Region where the bulk of the Āgamas were likely composed during the Pallava and early Cola periods.
geographic_locations.significance: The heartland for the development of the scriptural basis for sectarian Śaivism and Vaiṣṇavism.

geographic_locations.context: Site of Nāganikā's inscription.
geographic_locations.significance: Source of early epigraphic evidence on Sātavāhana religious practices.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Pertaining to the god Śiva; a follower of Śiva.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: One of the two main sectarian developments discussed in the chapter.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Pertaining to the god Viṣṇu; a follower of Viṣṇu.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: One of the two main sectarian developments discussed in the chapter.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Ascetic, monk (often referring to Buddhist, Jaina, or Ājīvika traditions).
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Mentioned in Aśoka's inscriptions as a group he showed concern for.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Priestly class in Vedic tradition.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Mentioned in Aśoka's inscriptions alongside śramaṇas.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Buddhist dome-shaped monumental structures.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Built by Sātavāhana kings near Kolhāpur.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Abode of Jina; a Jain temple.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Built by Ravi-varma at Palasikā.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: House of Viṣṇu; a temple to Viṣṇu.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Name for the rock-cut shrine at Bādāmi (Cave 3).

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: The Great Lord of the Kūṭa (peak); a name for Śiva.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The form of Śiva worshipped by Maṅgalīśa.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: A Jain shrine or temple (Kannada term).
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Built by Viṣṇuvardhana.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: A specific Vaiṣṇava tradition associated with Rāmānuja.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The faith Viṣṇuvardhana was rumored to have converted to.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: A Buddhist monastery.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Endowed by Vikramāditya VI at Dambaḷa.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.term: यो विश्वं वेदवेद्यं जननजलनिधेर्भागिनः पारदृश्वा । पौर्यापर्याविरुद्धं वचनमनुपमं निष्कलंकं यदियम्।
sanskrit_hindi_terms.transliteration: yo viśvaṁ vedavedyaṁ jananajalanidherbhāginaḥ pāradṛśvā । pauryāparyāviruddhaṁ vacanamanupamaṁ niṣkalaṁkaṁ yadiyam।
sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: He who is the seer of the yonder shore of the ocean of worldly existence, of which all the universe, knowable by the Vedas, is a part; whose word, unparalleled and stainless, is not opposed to the doctrine of former and later teachers.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: First part of a syncretic verse from an inscription assigned to 642 A.D.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.term: तं वन्दे साधुवन्द्यं सकलगुणनिधिं ध्वस्तदोषं द्विषन्तम्। बुद्धं वा वर्धमानं शतदलनिलयं वा केशवं वा शिवं वा ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.transliteration: taṁ vande sādhuvandyaṁ sakalaguṇanidhiṁ dhvastadoṣaṁ dviṣantam। buddhaṁ vā vardhamānaṁ śatadalanilayaṁ vā keśavaṁ vā śivaṁ vā ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: I praise that (principle), worthy of adoration by the good, the repository of all virtues, who has destroyed the fault of enmity, be it Buddha, or Vardhamāna (Jina), or he who resides in the hundred-petalled (lotus, i.e., Brahmā), or Keśava (Viṣṇu), or Śiva.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Second part of the syncretic verse from 642 A.D., showing equal reverence to multiple deities.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.term: यं शैवाः समुपासते शिव इति ब्रह्मोति वेदान्तिनः । बौद्धा बुद्ध इति प्रमाणपटवः कर्तेति नैयायिकाः। अर्हन्नित्यथ जैनशासनरता कर्मेति मीमांसकाः । सोऽयं वो विदधातु वांछितफलं त्रैलौक्यनाथो विभुः ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.transliteration: yaṁ śaivāḥ samupāsate śiva iti brahmeti vedāntinaḥ । bauddhā buddha iti pramāṇapaṭavaḥ karteti naiyāyikāḥ। arhannityatha jainaśāsanaratā karmeti mīmāṁsakāḥ । so'yaṁ vo vidadhātu vāṁchitaphalaṁ trailokyanātho vibhuḥ ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: May he, the lord of the three worlds the all powerful God, bestow on all of you the fulfillment of all desires, that one God whom the Śaivites worship as Śiva, the Vedāntins regard as Brahman, the Buddhists adore as the Buddha, the Naiyāyikas conceptualise as the Maker, the Jainas worship as Jina (Arhat) and the Mīmāṁsakas speak of as karma.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: A verse from a Hoysala period inscription in Belūr, explicitly stating different names for the same ultimate reality.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.term: जयन्ति यस्यावदातोऽपि भारती। विभूतयस्तिर्थकृतोऽपि नैह्निते शिवाय धात्रे सुगताय विष्णवे । जिनाय तस्मै सकलात्मने नमः ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.transliteration: jayanti yasyāvadāto'pi bhāratī। vibhūtayastirthakṛto'pi naihnite śivāya dhātre sugatāya viṣṇave । jināya tasmai sakalātmane namaḥ ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Victorious is his pure speech. The glories of the tirthakṛt are also not denied. Obeisance to Śiva, to the Creator (Brahmā), to Sugata (Buddha), to Viṣṇu. To that Jina, the soul of all, salutations.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: A verse from an inscription dated 1151 A.D. from Kaiḍāļa, paying obeisance to a single principle manifesting as multiple deities.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.term: यं वेदान्तविदो वदन्ति मनसः संकल्पभूतं शिवम् । ब्रह्मकं परमक्षरं तमजरं तंश्वामरं तद्विदुः । अन्ये तं शिवमेव बुद्धममलं त्वन्ये जिनं वामनम्। तस्मै सर्वमयैक्यकारणपते सर्वाय नित्याय नमः ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.transliteration: yaṁ vedāntavido vadanti manasaḥ saṁkalpabhūtaṁ śivam । brahmakaṁ paramakṣaraṁ tamajaraṁ taṁśvāmaraṁ tadviduḥ । anye taṁ śivameva buddhamamalaṁ tvanye jinaṁ vāmanam। tasmai sarvamayaikyakāraṇapate sarvāya nityāya namaḥ ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: He whom the knowers of Vedānta call Śiva, the embodiment of mind's resolve; they know him as Brahman, the supreme imperishable, the ageless, the immortal. Others (call) him Śiva himself, the stainless Buddha, and yet others Jina, Vāmana (Viṣṇu). To him, the lord who is the cause of the unity of all, to the all, the eternal, salutations.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: A prayer from the praśasti of Kokkalla-māharāja, describing the eternal God with various names.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Sects, schools of thought, religious systems.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Used to refer to the four major religious sects: Jainism, Buddhism, Śaivism, Vaiṣṇavism.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: An early Śaiva sect.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Listed as a division of Śaivism.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: A tantric, transgressive Śaiva sect.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Listed as a division of Śaivism.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.term: बौद्धं चाप्यार्हतं चैव शैवं पाशुपतं तथा । कापालं पांचरात्रंच षडेते समयाः स्मृताः ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.transliteration: bauddhaṁ cāpyārhataṁ caiva śaivaṁ pāśupataṁ tathā । kāpālaṁ pāṁcarātraṁca ṣaḍete samayāḥ smṛtāḥ ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Buddhism, as also Jainism, and Śaivism, Pāśupata, as well as Kāpālika and Pāñcarātra—these six are remembered as the sects (samayas).
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: A quote from the Vīrāgama (1, 77) listing six religious sects.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.term: बौद्धं चैवार्हतं चैव पांचरात्रं च शैवकम्। समयं चतुर्विधं स्यात्तु तत्तद्भदमनेकधा ।
sanskrit_hindi_terms.transliteration: bauddhaṁ caivārhataṁ caiva pāṁcarātraṁ ca śaivakam। samayaṁ caturvidhaṁ syāttu tattadbhadamanekadhā ।
sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Buddhism and Jainism, as well as Pāñcarātra and Śaivism. The sects would be of four kinds, and their various divisions are manifold.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: A quote from the Acintyāgama (40, 5-6) listing four major sects.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Supporter/Uplifter of the four sects.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: A title proudly claimed by many kings in their inscriptions.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Abode for the deities of the four sects.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Description of a temple in Kāḍiyūr from a 929 A.D. inscription.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Temples of Hari (Viṣṇu), Hara (Śiva), Kamalāsana (Brahmā), Vitarāga (Jina), and Buddha.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: A phrase from a Balligāme inscription (1129) describing a temple complex.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: The five streams irrigating the earth.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Metaphor used in the Balligāme inscription to describe the five doctrines.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Pertaining to the three divine persons (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva).
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Used to describe temples and worship dedicated to the Hindu trinity.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Self-born.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: An epithet for Brahmā.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Ancient lore; a genre of Hindu religious texts.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Source material for myths about Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Universal dissolution at the end of an aeon.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The time when Śiva acts as the destroyer.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Three-peaked mountain; a temple with three cells/shrines.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Architectural style for 'traipuruṣa' temples during the early Cālukya period.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Eulogy, panegyric.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: A type of inscription, such as that of Siddhi-nṛsiṁha-malla or Kokkalla-māharāja.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.term: ब्रह्मत्वे सृजते विश्वं स्थितौ पालयते हरिः । रुद्ररूपाय कल्पान्ते नमस्तुभ्यं त्रिमूर्तयो ।
sanskrit_hindi_terms.transliteration: brahmatve sṛjate viśvaṁ sthitau pālayate hariḥ । rudrarūpāya kalpānte namastubhyaṁ trimūrtayo ।
sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: In the form of Brahmā, you create the universe; in preservation, Hari protects it. In the form of Rudra at the end of the aeon (you destroy). Salutations to you, the one with three forms.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Verse from the praśasti of Nepali monarch Siddhi-nṛsiṁha-malla adoring the trinity.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.term: सर्गस्थितिलयहेतोर्विश्वस्य ब्रह्मविष्णुरुद्राणाम्। मूर्तित्रयं प्रदधते संसारभिदे नमो विभवे ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.transliteration: sargasthitilayahetorviśvasya brahmaviṣṇurudrāṇām। mūrtitrayaṁ pradadhate saṁsārabhide namo vibhave ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: For the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction of the universe, (you) assume the three forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. Salutations to the mighty one who breaks the cycle of worldly existence.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: A similar verse from a stone inscription in Śiva's temple in Madha-pura.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Aniconic representations of Śiva.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The Trikūṭeśvara temple at Gadag has three, representing Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.term: लक्ष्मीवल्लभ-शैलजादयितयोरद्वैतलीलगृहम्। प्रद्युम्नेश्वर-शब्दलांछनमधिष्ठानं नमुस्कुर्महे । यत्रालिगंमभंग-कातरतया स्थित्वान्तरे कान्तयो-र्देवीभ्यां कथमप्यभिन्नतनुता शिल्पेऽन्तरायः कृतः ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.transliteration: lakṣmīvallabha-śailajādayitayoradvaitalīlagṛham। pradyumneśvara-śabdalāṁchanamadhiṣṭhānaṁ namaskurmahe । yatrāliṁgamabhaṁga-kātaratayā sthitvāntare kāntayo-rdevībhyāṁ kathamapyabhinnatanutā śilpe'ntarāyaḥ kṛtaḥ ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: We bow to the abode marked by the word Pradyumneśvara, the house of non-dual sport of the beloved of Lakṣmī (Viṣṇu) and the beloved of the daughter of the mountain (Śiva). Where, standing between the two consorts (Lakṣmī and Pārvatī), who were afraid of an embrace being broken, the sculptor somehow created a separation, preventing their non-different bodies.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: An 11th-century inscription from Bengal describing a joint Śiva-Viṣṇu temple.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: House of non-dual sport/play.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Description of the Pradyumneśvara temple.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: A composite form of Viṣṇu (Hari) and Śiva (Hara).
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: A syncretic icon that came into vogue as separate Śaiva/Vaiṣṇava identities grew.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Another name for the composite form of Śiva (Śaṅkara) and Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa).
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Synonym for Hari-Hara.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Traditional doctrines, scriptures; specifically sectarian texts on temple-worship.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The prescriptive texts that crystallized the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava cults.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Āgamas relating to Śiva.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The specific texts for the Śaiva sect.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Āgamas relating to Viṣṇu.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The specific texts for the Vaiṣṇava sect.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: The 'Great Vehicle', a major branch of Buddhism.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Its sects flourished and developed their own Āgamas and pantheon.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Ford-makers; the 24 enlightened spiritual guides in Jainism.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The primary figures of worship prescribed in Jaina-āgamas.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Male/female nature spirits, often attendant deities.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Their worship was also prescribed in Jaina-āgamas.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Buddhist Āgamas.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Form part of Vajrayāna-tantras.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Tantric texts of the 'Diamond Vehicle' school of Buddhism.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The corpus to which Bauddha-āgamas belong.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Enlightenment-beings; compassionate beings in Mahāyāna Buddhism.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Their worship (e.g., Avalokiteśvara) is detailed in Bauddha-āgamas.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Power, energy; the divine feminine principle, the mother goddess.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Her worship is noted as ancient but formalized in temples later.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Lord of Beasts/Souls, an epithet of Śiva.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Invoked in the opening of Hāla's Gāthā-saptaśatī.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.term: पसुवइणो रोसारुणपडिमासंकांत गोरिमुहअन्दं। गहिअग्धपंकअं विअ संझासलिलांजलिं णमह ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.transliteration: pasuvaiṇo rosāruṇapaḍimāsaṁkāṁta gorimahaandaṁ। gahiagghapaṁkaaṁ via saṁjhāsalilāṁjaliṁ ṇamaha ॥
sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: (Sanskrit Chhaya: īpaśupate roṣāruṇapratimāsaṁkrāntagaurīmukhacandram। gṛhītārdhapaṅkajamiva sandhyāsalilāñjaliṁ namatā ||) Bow down to the handful of evening twilight water of Paśupati, which is like a half-plucked lotus, with the moon of Gaurī's face reflected in it, reddened by his anger.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: Prakrit verse from Hāla's Gāthā-saptaśatī invoking Śiva and Gauri.

quotations.quote: Strife on account of bigotry, fanaticism and discrimination in the name of religion has been rare and unusual.
quotations.context: Opening paragraph statement about India's history of religious tolerance.

quotations.quote: यो विश्वं वेदवेद्यं जननजलनिधेर्भागिनः पारदृश्वा । पौर्यापर्याविरुद्धं वचनमनुपमं निष्कलंकं यदियम्। तं वन्दे साधुवन्द्यं सकलगुणनिधिं ध्वस्तदोषं द्विषन्तम्। बुद्धं वा वर्धमानं शतदलनिलयं वा केशवं वा शिवं वा ॥
quotations.context: A verse paying obeisance to a single principle manifesting as Buddha, Vardhamāna, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Śiva.

quotations.quote: यं शैवाः समुपासते शिव इति ब्रह्मोति वेदान्तिनः । बौद्धा बुद्ध इति प्रमाणपटवः कर्तेति नैयायिकाः। अर्हन्नित्यथ जैनशासनरता कर्मेति मीमांसकाः । सोऽयं वो विदधातु वांछितफलं त्रैलौक्यनाथो विभुः ॥
quotations.source: Inscription of the Hoysaḷa period in Belūr in Karnataka
quotations.context: A verse stating that various sects worship the same single God under different names and concepts.

quotations.quote: "May he, the lord of the three worlds the all powerful God, bestow on all of you the fulfillment of all desires, that one God whom the Śaivites worship as Śiva, the Vedāntins regard as Brahman, the Buddhists adore as the Buddha, the Naiyāyikas conceptualise as the Maker, the Jainas worship as Jina (Arhat) and the Mīmāmsakas speak of as karma".
quotations.source: Author's translation of the Belūr inscription
quotations.context: English translation of the above Sanskrit verse.

quotations.quote: जयन्ति यस्यावदातोऽपि भारती। विभूतयस्तिर्थकृतोऽपि नैह्निते शिवाय धात्रे सुगताय विष्णवे । जिनाय तस्मै सकलात्मने नमः ॥
quotations.source: Inscription dated 1151 A.D. from Kaidāļa (Tumkur district)
quotations.context: A verse paying obeisance to the 'one principle' which manifests as Śiva, Brahmā, Sugata (Buddha), Viṣṇu, and Jina.

quotations.quote: यं वेदान्तविदो वदन्ति मनसः संकल्पभूतं शिवम् । ब्रह्मकं परमक्षरं तमजरं तंश्वामरं तद्विदुः । अन्ये तं शिवमेव बुद्धममलं त्वन्ये जिनं वामनम्। तस्मै सर्वमयैक्यकारणपते सर्वाय नित्याय नमः ॥
quotations.context: A prayer to the all-comprehensive eternal God described by various names.

quotations.quote: बौद्धं चाप्यार्हतं चैव शैवं पाशुपतं तथा । कापालं पांचरात्रंच षडेते समयाः स्मृताः ॥
quotations.context: A verse listing six religious sects (samayas).

quotations.quote: बौद्धं चैवार्हतं चैव पांचरात्रं च शैवकम्। समयं चतुर्विधं स्यात्तु तत्तद्भदमनेकधा ।
quotations.context: A verse listing four major religious sects with many subdivisions.
A title claimed by many kings.
Description of a temple for deities of four sects.
Name for a temple complex housing shrines for five faiths.
Metaphorical description of the five doctrines.

quotations.quote: ब्रह्मत्वे सृजते विश्वं स्थितौ पालयते हरिः । रुद्ररूपाय कल्पान्ते नमस्तुभ्यं त्रिमूर्तयो ।
quotations.context: Verse adoring the three forms of the one god responsible for creation, preservation, and destruction.

quotations.quote: सर्गस्थितिलयहेतोर्विश्वस्य ब्रह्मविष्णुरुद्राणाम्। मूर्तित्रयं प्रदधते संसारभिदे नमो विभवे ॥
quotations.source: Stone-inscription in Śiva's temple in Madha-pura
quotations.context: A similar verse adoring the trinity.

quotations.quote: लक्ष्मीवल्लभ-शैलजादयितयोरद्वैतलीलगृहम्। प्रद्युम्नेश्वर-शब्दलांछनमधिष्ठानं नमुस्कुर्महे । यत्रालिगंमभंग-कातरतया स्थित्वान्तरे कान्तयो-र्देवीभ्यां कथमप्यभिन्नतनुता शिल्पेऽन्तरायः कृतः ॥
quotations.source: Eleventh century inscription from Devpād village, Bengal
quotations.context: Describes a temple dedicated to Pradyumneśvara (a composite Śiva-Viṣṇu form).

quotations.quote: पसुवइणो रोसारुणपडिमासंकांत गोरिमुहअन्दं। गहिअग्धपंकअं विअ संझासलिलांजलिं णमह ॥
quotations.context: Invocation to Śiva (Paśupati) as the husband of Gauri.

controversial_points: The assertion on page 1 that 'Strife on account of bigotry, fanaticism and discrimination in the name of religion has been rare and unusual' presents a highly idealized view of Indian history, which many historians would contest by pointing to various instances of sectarian conflict.

On page 2, the author's claim that there is 'hardly any historical evidence' for Aśoka's conversion to Buddhism is a fringe view. While the nature of his conversion is debated, the influence of Buddhism on his policies and his patronage of it, as evidenced by his edicts, is widely accepted as substantial.

On page 3, the statement that the story of Hoysala king Viṣṇuvardhana's conversion to Śrīvaiṣṇavism by Rāmānuja 'is without foundation' dismisses a long-held traditional account. While its historicity is a subject of scholarly debate, stating it is entirely 'without foundation' is a strong, debatable claim.
alternative_viewpoints: The mainstream historical view accepts Aśoka's conversion to or strong adherence to Buddhism following the Kalinga war, citing the Edicts of Aśoka as primary evidence of his promotion of Dhamma (Dharma) based on Buddhist principles.

The traditional Śrīvaiṣṇava accounts hold that Viṣṇuvardhana's conversion was a pivotal event, marking the establishment of Śrīvaiṣṇavism in Karnataka. While some modern historians question the details, they acknowledge Rāmānuja's significant influence in the region during that period, making the tradition plausible to some extent.
